result.summary:
TRUTH REVIEW of the MYEZ legal set at 10135306 (read-only; engineering due diligence, not legal advice; counsel_review=false in tests/fixtures/legal_fill_in_u8.json:9, so no lawyer has reviewed these texts yet).

MEASURED 2026-10-11: (1) The live pages match the repo exactly. GET /api/v1/legal/{privacy,terms}[?lang=ar] returns content byte-equal to the four markdown files at 10135306. Every markdown line of 20 characters or more appears in getmyez.com/{privacy,terms,ar/privacy,ar/terms}.html. (2) The getmyez.com apex answers with 'Server: railway-hikari', no cf-ray and HSTS. So the apex is NOT proxied by Cloudflare today, which contradicts the orchestrator fact. However, a random subdomain still resolves to Cloudflare (172.67.189.201 / 104.21.41.71) through the proxied wildcard record. (3) The landing pages load only Google Fonts. They have no analytics and no cookies.

The English documents are largely truthful against the code: 043 deletion, store=False, no identity sent to OpenAI, the limits 3/3/10, referral 3/5/7 days, certificate pinning, Keychain, the device fingerprint, Sentry in the EU, no ad SDK. The Arabic text is a faithful translation.

The real exposures are in practices and promises:
(a) 'We do not sell your personal data' sits beside an OpenAI data-sharing programme that pays in complimentary tokens. That programme receives user photos and the data of 13-17-year-olds.
(b) AI consent lives only on the device. The backend never checks it, so a direct API call gets processed and shared without consent, and the owner cannot prove consent.
(c) The contract and transfer promises in s5/s7 are probably not backed by signed DPAs or by a PDPL transfer basis.
(d) Mail to privacy@ and support@ lands in a personal Gmail inbox that the policy does not name.
(e) In-app and landing copy over-promises: 'never share your name/email, not ever', 'never share your budget', 'authorized retailers'.
(f) Retention is 'no fixed period' for IP and email-hash records.
(g) The public repo, keys whose rotation is owed, the anon-readable views and the wildcard DNS record are abuse and reputation vectors.

ON SELLING DATA: the current clause (sell or license only aggregated or anonymised statistics, never personal data) is the defensible limit. Selling personal data would break Apple 5.1.2(i), which says data 'may only be shared with third parties to improve the app or serve advertising'. It would also make the app Tracking (ATT prompt, label change) and would need fresh explicit consent under the PDPLs. Collecting as broadly as big companies do is lawful only with the same apparatus behind it: per-purpose legal bases, signed DPAs, transfer mechanisms, fixed retention and easy consent withdrawal. Those are the gaps listed below.

FREE WITH LIMITS: already stated in ToS s4, EN and AR ('Use of MYEZ is free ... 3 a day and up to 10 a month, after 3 introductory comparisons ... sells no subscriptions'). No change is needed. Optionally, add that the introductory comparisons count toward the monthly window.

ASIDE on the user's question: inviting Ahmed Jameel (Users and Access, Developer role) is an Account Holder or Admin action that is independent of screenshots, build and Add for Review. As far as I know it is not a submission prerequisite (I did not verify this against Apple's documentation).

Primary sources used:
- Apple App Review Guidelines 5.1.1(ii), 5.1.2(i) (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/).
- Apple 'Offering account deletion in your app' (https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/).
- OpenAI help article 10306912 (https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10306912-sharing-feedback-evaluation-and-fine-tuning-data-and-api-inputs-and-outputs-with-openai). The live page returned 403, so the content comes from the search-indexed copy and is UNVERIFIED live.

The Bahrain PDPL primary text was NOT retrievable: pdp.gov.bh returned 403, and the MOH PDF could not be parsed. Every Bahrain or Saudi article reference below is UNVERIFIED and comes from secondary summaries (lexmundi, PwC). The OpenAI and Google privacy policy pages returned 403, so the big-company comparison is not quoted.

Files written: only scratch copies under C:/Users/SYNACK~1/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-SynAckITPC-Documents-AI/b66a80d9-2bd6-44b5-bde6-1370a9fa1121/scratchpad/truth/ (git-show extracts, live/ fetches, and cmp.py sha256 fb917759a9c3610247291c96382411316d1f2c13b4cda6d3435743050e0c1704). Nothing was written in any repository or worktree.

findings.title: Possible unrotated leaked keys would falsify the s13 security claims
findings.where: CLAUDE.md:614,627 (owner list: 'rotate the eight leaked keys ... then ADMIN_API_KEY'); CLAUDE.md:681 (ADMIN_API_KEY was exposed in Sentry frame locals; a live CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN with no readers); privacy_policy.md s13
findings.evidence: The repo records rotation as owed and has no record that it was done. Which eight keys leaked is not named in the files I read. It is UNVERIFIED whether the Supabase service-role key is among them. The repo is public.
findings.why_it_matters: If any still-valid key gives database or admin reach (Supabase service role, ADMIN_API_KEY, Cloudflare), every user's email, profile, demographics and history is exposed. That would be a reportable breach, and it makes 'Administrative functions require a secret key' meaningless.
findings.fix: Before submission the owner rotates every key on the list plus ADMIN_API_KEY, deletes the unused Cloudflare token, and records the date in the repo. Then grep the git history of the public repo for each key's prefix to confirm none is still valid.

findings.title: 'We do not sell your personal data' while inputs are traded to OpenAI for free tokens
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s2 ('We do not sell your personal data ... section 4 describes what OpenAI may do'), s4 para 3; decision D3 = C (memory: 'OpenAI sharing stays ON (free daily tokens)')
findings.evidence: OpenAI's help article (search-indexed copy; live page 403) says eligible organisations receive 'daily complimentary tokens on traffic shared with OpenAI'. The policy discloses the training use but not the consideration. The app shares photos, typed products, linked page text, preferences, country and region.
findings.why_it_matters: A journalist or claimant can frame this as 'MYEZ swaps your photos for free AI credits' and contrast it with the 'we do not sell' sentence. 'Sale' is not a defined term in the GCC laws (UNVERIFIED), but a misleading-statement claim does not need the definition. This is the single most quotable weakness.
findings.fix: Choose one. (A) Turn organisation data sharing OFF. Then delete the s4 programme paragraph and the consent-sheet training sentence, and bump AI_CONSENT_VERSION. (B) Keep it ON and state the exchange plainly in s2 and s4 (wording below). Also drop the bare 'We do not sell your personal data' in favour of the qualified sentence.
findings.proposed_wording_en: We do not sell your personal data to data brokers or advertisers. We do take part in OpenAI's data-sharing programme: OpenAI may use the inputs we send it and the outputs it generates to evaluate and train its models, and in return OpenAI gives us some free use of its service (section 4).

findings.title: Photos and minors' inputs go into OpenAI's training programme
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s4; app/api/image_routes.py:217-236,310 (image bytes go to identify_products); ToS s3 (13+); aiConsent.body
findings.evidence: The image route forwards user photos to OpenAI Vision under the organisation-wide sharing setting. OpenAI's help article advises 'do not include any sensitive, confidential, or proprietary information' in shared data (search-indexed copy). Users aged 13+ are admitted. Photos can contain faces, home interiors or documents.
findings.why_it_matters: Training on minors' data and on incidental images of people is the scenario most likely to draw regulator or press attention. Apple 5.1.2(i) also says data may only be shared with third parties 'to improve the app or serve advertising'. Training OpenAI's own models arguably falls outside that, even with permission, so there is a review risk.
findings.fix: Route /image/identify (and ideally all calls) through a separate OpenAI project with data sharing OFF; the article says sharing is managed per project or organisation. Alternatively turn sharing off for everyone. Update s4 and the consent sheet to match. At minimum, add a camera hint telling users not to photograph people.

findings.title: AI consent is stored only on the device; the backend never checks it
findings.where: SmartCompareApp/src/services/aiConsent.ts:12-22 (AsyncStorage '@qaren_ai_consent_<userId>'); no ai_consent reference anywhere in app/
findings.evidence: The grep for ai_consent/AI_CONSENT in app/ returns nothing. The compare, image and url routes send data to OpenAI for any authenticated caller. The policy (s3.6, s4) names that permission as the legal basis for the OpenAI sharing.
findings.why_it_matters: The controller cannot show when or whether a user consented. Any authenticated request outside the app's consent gate is processed and shared without consent: direct API use (the repo is public, so the endpoints are documented) or a future client bug. Under PDPL-style laws the controller must be able to demonstrate consent (UNVERIFIED article).
findings.fix: Record {ai_consent_version, ai_consent_at} on public.users through an authenticated endpoint called when the user taps Agree. Refuse compare, image and url calls with 4xx when the current version is absent, behind a flag. Add both columns to the 043 erasure list.

findings.title: The contract-protection and transfer promises in s5/s7 are probably unbacked
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s5 ('we require each of them to protect it at least as well as this policy does'); s7 ('We transfer data only to providers that are required by contract to protect it'); legal_fill_in_u8.json:54-56 (TRANSFER_BASIS null, counsel_review false)
findings.evidence: The repo has no record of a signed or accepted DPA with Serper, Bright Data, Firecrawl, Scrape.do, Upstash, Railway, Expo or Cloudflare. Supabase, OpenAI and Sentry offer click-through DPAs, but whether they were accepted is UNVERIFIED. Secondary summaries of Bahrain PDPL Art. 12-13 (primary text UNVERIFIED) say a transfer abroad needs an adequate country on the Authority's list, Authority authorisation, or an exception such as explicit consent or contract necessity. 'Required by contract' alone is not one of those.
findings.why_it_matters: These are specific, checkable promises. A complainant asking 'show me the contract' finds none, and the transfer clause may name a basis the law does not recognise.
findings.fix: Owner: accept or download the DPAs that exist (Supabase, OpenAI, Sentry, Upstash, Railway, Expo, Cloudflare) and record them. Counsel: choose the PDPL transfer basis; likely necessity for the contract with the user plus explicit consent for the OpenAI programme. Until then, soften the text to what is true.
findings.proposed_wording_en: Our providers process data outside Bahrain, including in the United States, Germany, India and Singapore. We send them only the data each needs to provide its service to us, and we use providers that commit, in their terms or data-processing agreements, to protect it.

findings.title: Mail to privacy@ and support@ lands in a personal Gmail inbox the policy does not name
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s5 ('Cloudflare: delivers the email you send to our addresses'); NEXT_SESSION_PROMPT_S77.md:11 and ASC packet :441 (forward to a personal Gmail address)
findings.evidence: Cloudflare Email Routing forwards both mailboxes to a consumer Gmail account. Google therefore stores every support and privacy request (identity, the request text, attachments) with no fixed retention.
findings.why_it_matters: This is an undisclosed recipient of exactly the most sensitive mail: data-subject requests. Using a consumer account rather than a business account also weakens the s5 processor promise.
findings.fix: Name Google (Gmail) in s5 and s7 as the inbox host, or move the mailboxes to a business mail service with a DPA. State a retention period for support mail.
findings.proposed_wording_en: Cloudflare and Google: Cloudflare routes the email you send to our addresses, and Google (Gmail) stores it in our inbox.

findings.title: In-app privacy copy over-promises ('not now, not ever'; 'never share your budget')
findings.where: SmartCompareApp/src/i18n/en.json onboarding.s5.privacy_never_body 'Your name. Your email. Not now, not ever.'; referrals.share.privacyNote 'We never share your budget or personal answers.' (plus the AR twins)
findings.evidence: Policy s5 says invitees see your display name and an inviter's notification can show it. Email goes to Supabase, Cloudflare and Gmail, and may be disclosed 'where the law requires'. Budget level is sent to OpenAI and may be used for training (aiConsent.body).
findings.why_it_matters: These absolute statements contradict the published policy and the consent sheet. They are the lines a reviewer or claimant would quote.
findings.fix: Rewrite both strings with an OTA (EN + AR) and keep the jest copy pins in sync.
findings.proposed_wording_en: privacy_never_body: 'We never send your name or email to OpenAI, and we never sell them.' referrals.share.privacyNote: 'People you share with never see your budget or personal answers.'

findings.title: Landing page says prices are 'sourced from authorized retailers'
findings.where: https://getmyez.com/ (live, measured 2026-10-11): 'Compare electronics, supplements, fragrances, fashion, and more — sourced from authorized retailers across the region.'
findings.evidence: The backend reaches marketplaces and general stores (domains in app/: amazon.*, aliexpress.com, temu.com, ebay.com, noon.com and others). No authorisation status is checked.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Authorized retailer' is a specific commercial claim. Brands or consumer-protection bodies can challenge it, and it conflicts with ToS s7 ('third-party retailers').
findings.fix: Replace it with 'with prices from retailers across the region' (EN + AR) and redeploy the landing.

findings.title: Apple token revocation on account deletion is deferred (U11)
findings.where: app/services/auth_service.py:1008-1022 (delete_user_account: cascade, cache purge, auth delete; no Apple REST call); ASC packet s5 'SIWA token revocation on deletion is U11 = A (after launch)'
findings.evidence: Apple: apps that support Sign in with Apple 'should use the Sign in with Apple REST API to revoke user tokens' (https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/).
findings.why_it_matters: This is a known App Review rejection reason under 5.1.1(v), and it leaves the app linked under the user's Apple ID after the user deleted the account.
findings.fix: Implement token revocation (it needs the SIWA key from packet s1.4), or accept the review risk knowingly.

findings.title: AI permission can be withdrawn only by deleting the whole account
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s4 para 2 and s10; legal_fill_in_u8.json _values_comment ('there is no in-App withdrawal control')
findings.evidence: Apple 5.1.1(ii): 'Apps must also provide the customer with an easily accessible and understandable way to withdraw consent.' The only routes are Delete account or an email.
findings.why_it_matters: Making account deletion the price of withdrawing consent can be read as bundled, non-free consent under the PDPLs (counsel) and as weak under 5.1.1(ii). It also hides the fact that history is lost.
findings.fix: Add a 'Withdraw AI permission' row in Profile > Privacy that clears the record locally and on the server (T04) and blocks compares until re-granted. Update s4 and s10.

findings.title: 'No fixed period' retention for IP and email-hash records and unlinked searches
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s8 bullets 4-5, s9; app/api/auth_routes.py:689-692,1066-1069 (email_hash = sha256(email.lower())[:16], unsalted)
findings.evidence: Lockout and failed-sign-in audit rows and anonymous search_logs rows have no cleanup. The fill-in comment ties a fixed period to migration 044, which is not merged. An unsalted, truncated SHA-256 of an email is reversible by dictionary, so it remains personal data.
findings.why_it_matters: Storage limitation is a core PDPL principle. Apple 5.1.1(i) asks the policy to 'Explain its data retention/deletion policies'. Indefinite IP retention is an easy complaint to file.
findings.fix: Ship 044 (for example 12 months for audit rows and anonymous logs) with a scheduled cleanup, then fill in the period. Switch the email hash to an HMAC keyed by a server secret.

findings.title: Policies name only the Bahrain and Saudi regulators; no notification or registration is recorded
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s10 last paragraph; legal_fill_in_u8.json:9 counsel_review=false; app availability: the 6 GCC states
findings.evidence: Secondary sources (UNVERIFIED) indicate Bahrain PDPL requires notifying the PDP Authority before automated processing. Saudi PDPL applies to processing of KSA residents' data from abroad, possibly with registration or representative duties (UNVERIFIED). Oman RD 6/2022, Qatar Law 13/2016 and UAE FDL 45/2021 users get no complaint route.
findings.why_it_matters: Launching in 6 jurisdictions without a counsel pass leaves unknown statutory gaps; the controller is an individual and is personally liable.
findings.fix: A one-off GCC counsel review covering the notification or registration duties, the transfer basis (T05), the minors rule (T13) and the regulator list. Then set counsel_review true and re-run the fill-in.

findings.title: No parental-consent mechanism although the ToS requires guardian agreement for minors
findings.where: terms_of_service.md s3; privacy_policy.md s12; en.json auth.consent.prefix 'I am 13 or older and I agree to the'
findings.evidence: The ToS says a guardian must agree for users under the age of majority (18 in KSA; Bahrain's age of majority is UNVERIFIED), but the sign-up checkbox only attests 13+. The minors' data then joins the OpenAI programme (T03).
findings.why_it_matters: A minor's contract and consent may be voidable, and minors' data being used for AI training draws the most scrutiny.
findings.fix: Either change the minimum age to 18 (ToS, policy s12, age rating, checkbox), or change the checkbox to 'I am 13 or older and, if I am under 18, my parent or guardian agrees' and exclude under-18s from the OpenAI sharing. Counsel to pick.

findings.title: The public GitHub repo exposes the owner's contact details and the security posture
findings.where: Repo KGRddhs/smartcompare-backend (public per CLAUDE.md:536; not re-measured); docs/investigations/2026-10-10-session-76-state/NEXT_SESSION_PROMPT_S76.md:10 and ledger.md:23 (personal phone number and Gmail); CLAUDE.md flag states (ENABLE_PROXY_AWARE_RATELIMIT OFF, one shared limiter bucket)
findings.evidence: The session docs carry the review contact's phone number and personal email. CLAUDE.md documents which abuse defences are off. Every endpoint and the fingerprint design are readable.
findings.why_it_matters: It gives attackers a map for account farming, cost abuse and phishing of the owner. It also hands critics a ready narrative about the app's privacy posture.
findings.fix: Make the repo private (owner). If it must stay public, purge personal contact data from docs and history.

findings.title: Wildcard DNS '*.getmyez.com' points through Cloudflare to a third-party IP
findings.where: ledger.md:53 (snapshot: '*.getmyez.com A 91.195.240.94 proxied'); measured 2026-10-11: a random subdomain resolves to Cloudflare 172.67.189.201 / 104.21.41.71
findings.evidence: Any subdomain under the brand is served from a non-MYEZ origin (likely a parking host; the content was not fetched, per the rules). The apex itself is now DNS-only to Railway (Server: railway-hikari, no cf-ray).
findings.why_it_matters: Brand subdomains showing third-party parking or ad content are a phishing and credibility risk. Cloudflare would also see visitors' IPs on those hosts, which the policy does not cover.
findings.fix: Delete the wildcard A record in Cloudflare and keep only the apex, www and the mail records.

findings.title: Supabase free plan with no backups
findings.where: Orchestrator fact (ap-south-1, free plan, NO backups); privacy_policy.md s8 last bullet ('Copies in our providers' backups ... deleted on their schedules')
findings.evidence: The project has no recoverable backup. Free projects can also be paused by the provider (UNVERIFIED current policy).
findings.why_it_matters: Losing all accounts and history is an integrity and availability failure under 'appropriate security measures'. It would also be a public incident. The backup sentence implies a safety net that does not exist.
findings.fix: Upgrade to Supabase Pro (already on the owner list), which includes daily backups. Then the s8 sentence becomes accurate.

findings.title: Free-tier account farming and cost abuse
findings.where: app/services/usage_service.py:138-149 (per-account tiers); app/middleware/rate_limiter.py:24-70 (proxy-aware key OFF: one limiter bucket per route); deviceFingerprint.ts (nonce in Keychain)
findings.evidence: Every new email gets 3 lifetime-free comparisons and then 3/day. The device fingerprint resets with a new device or a wipe. Whether email verification is enforced before compares is UNVERIFIED. CLAUDE.md:536 records 322 anonymous compares from 155 addresses with no 429 before the auth requirement.
findings.why_it_matters: Scripted sign-ups can burn OpenAI, Serper and Bright Data spend. ToS s3 forbids automated accounts, but nothing enforces it.
findings.fix: Require a verified email before the first compare. Add a global daily spend ceiling (the breaker exists). Keep the per-device lifetime cap on sign-ups. Fix the XFF anchor before enabling ENABLE_PROXY_AWARE_RATELIMIT (CLAUDE.md:362).

findings.title: Three SECURITY DEFINER cohort views are readable with the public anon key
findings.where: migrations/013_demographics_cohort.sql:23-57 (vw_cohort_match_rate, vw_cohort_persona_distribution, vw_cohort_feedback_lift)
findings.evidence: These return daily user totals, persona counts and feedback rates (aggregate only; measured by the orchestrator 2026-10-11). No individual rows are exposed.
findings.why_it_matters: They leak business metrics (sign-ups per day). They also undercut the 'administrative functions require a secret key' posture. This is not personal data.
findings.fix: Migration: REVOKE SELECT on the three views FROM anon, authenticated, or recreate them WITH (security_invoker = true).

findings.title: Policy says country may be set from network location; the ASC label declares no location
findings.where: privacy_policy.md s3.3 ('which we may set from ... your network location'); app/api/auth_routes.py:1509-1517 (_derive_country reads cf-ipcountry); ASC packet s4 (Coarse Location unticked)
findings.evidence: The API is called on the Railway host directly (certificatePinning.ts BACKEND_HOST), not through Cloudflare. So cf-ipcountry is never added by Cloudflare; the header is client-supplied and spoofable, and an absent header defaults to 'Bahrain'.
findings.why_it_matters: The policy describes a collection that never happens and conflicts with the published label (no Coarse Location). The code path also accepts a forged header.
findings.fix: Remove the cf-ipcountry read and default to 'Bahrain', and delete 'and your network location' (EN + AR). Alternatively, if the API ever moves behind Cloudflare, declare Coarse Location first (inventory PM-8).

findings.title: The 'Other Purposes' rows of the published label are not recorded in the repo
findings.where: ASC_SUBMISSION_PACKET_S76.md s4 (Other Purposes on 3 rows: Photos, Other User Content, Other Data Types); orchestrator fact (published with Other Purposes on 5 rows); docs/privacy-data-inventory.md and app.json manifest (none)
findings.evidence: The three sources disagree on which rows carry Other Purposes.
findings.why_it_matters: The next label edit or manifest rebuild could drop a disclosure that is live today.
findings.fix: Record the 5 published rows in the packet and inventory notes. Add them to the manifest at the next native build if desired, together with the c3/c5 jest pins.

findings.title: Consent sheet omits two s4 facts (cohort patterns, withdrawal route)
findings.where: en.json aiConsent.body vs privacy_policy.md s4
findings.evidence: The sheet does not mention 'general patterns from people whose survey answers are similar to yours' (sent when ENABLE_COHORT_PERSONALIZATION is on; extraction_service.py:1974-2057). It also does not say how to withdraw. The sheet does link to the policy.
findings.why_it_matters: The consent is less specific than the policy it relies on; this is minor because of the link.
findings.fix: Fold both into the next AI_CONSENT_VERSION bump (together with T02/T03/T10), EN + AR.

findings.title: Sign-in data minimisation (Apple FULL_NAME unused, Google profile stored by Supabase)
findings.where: SmartCompareApp/src/services/authService.ts:1038-1040 (requests FULL_NAME, never sent to backend: body {provider,id_token,nonce}); Supabase signInWithIdToken stores Google name and picture in auth.users metadata (UNVERIFIED live)
findings.evidence: The Apple name scope is requested but unused. Policy s3.1 does not list the Google name and picture as stored.
findings.why_it_matters: Collecting what you do not use contradicts minimisation, and the Google profile picture is an undisclosed stored item.
findings.fix: Drop the FULL_NAME scope at the next native build. Add 'and, if you use Google Sign-In, the name and profile picture Google shares, kept by our sign-in provider' to s3.1.

findings.title: Zyte and pasted-link query strings are uncovered
findings.where: app/services/structured_comparison_service.py:6652-6657 (Zyte called on the request path when ENABLE_ZYTE_RENDER is on; prod value UNVERIFIED); processors.json _comment calls Zyte off-clock only; privacy s5 'never your identity'
findings.evidence: Zyte is not named in s5. Pasted URLs are fetched by Firecrawl and Scrape.do and their text goes to OpenAI. Whether query strings (which can carry session or affiliate identifiers) are stripped is UNVERIFIED.
findings.why_it_matters: These are small accuracy gaps in the recipient list and in the 'never your identity' claim.
findings.fix: Confirm ENABLE_ZYTE_RENDER is off on web (otherwise add Zyte to s5). Strip non-essential query parameters from pasted URLs before fetching.

findings.title: ToS has no language-precedence, indemnity or discontinuation clause
findings.where: terms_of_service.md s12-s15 (and AR)
findings.evidence: There is no clause saying which version governs if the EN and AR texts differ. There is no user indemnity and no right to modify or discontinue the service. Scraping and hotlinking of retailer content (prices, review summaries, product images loaded from retailer servers) rests on the ASC Content Rights call, which is still open.
findings.why_it_matters: These are standard defensive clauses; their absence widens dispute exposure for an individual controller.
findings.fix: Counsel adds: 'If the English and Arabic versions differ, the [English] version prevails'; a user indemnity for misuse; 'we may change, suspend or discontinue the App'. The owner answers Content Rights.

findings.title: Live legal pages and the API equal the markdown at 10135306
findings.where: getmyez.com/{privacy,terms,ar/privacy,ar/terms}.html; /api/v1/legal/{privacy,terms}[?lang=ar]
findings.evidence: The API content is byte-equal to all four .md files. The landing pages render every markdown line (0 of 90/51/84/48 missing). The support page shows the controller, the address and support@getmyez.com.
findings.why_it_matters: What reviewers and users read is what was reviewed.
findings.fix: none

findings.title: OpenAI calls use store=False and send no identity or demographics
findings.where: app/services/api_budget_service.py:977-980 (the single chat chokepoint forces store=False, extra_body too); extraction_service.py:1974-2057 (USER CONTEXT = Country/Language/Region plus cohort modal, no age or gender); structured_comparison_service.py:4228-4231 (behaviour profile goes to deterministic scoring only)
findings.evidence: The only other OpenAI call is moderations.create (content_safety_service.py:252), which is not stored.
findings.why_it_matters: Confirms policy s4 ('we never send your age group or gender themselves'; no name, email or account id; behaviour profile not sent).
findings.fix: none

findings.title: Account deletion matches policy s9 (migration 043)
findings.where: migrations/043_delete_user_cascade_full_erasure.sql (DELETEs on 11 tables, admin_audit_log ip_address NULLed, 25 users columns erased); app/services/auth_service.py:984-1022 (5 per-user Redis keys purged, then auth.admin.delete_user)
findings.evidence: Usage counters keep their 24 h / 32 d TTLs (usage_service.py:250,261). The applied state and POSTCHECK were recorded by the orchestrator (ledger.md:42).
findings.why_it_matters: Supports the s9 claims and Apple 5.1.1(v).
findings.fix: none

findings.title: Free limits and referral numbers in ToS s4 and s9 match the code (EN + AR)
findings.where: app/services/usage_service.py:138-149 (free: lifetime 3, daily 3, monthly 10; premium 10/70 with no purchase path); referral_service.py:40,46 (LIFETIME_CAP 3, BONUS_EXPIRY_DAYS 7); ToS s4 'sells no subscriptions or in-app purchases'
findings.evidence: The AR terms carry the same digits (s4: 3, 10, 3; s9: 3, 5, 7). Nuance: the 3 introductory comparisons also advance the daily and monthly counters (usage_service.py:360-364).
findings.why_it_matters: The 'free with rate limits' note the owner asked for is already published.

findings.title: Selling even aggregated statistics needs counsel against Apple DPLA 3.3.3(B) and guideline 5.1.2(i) before the first deal

findings.evidence: DPLA 3.3.3(B): data may be collected "only to provide a service or function that is directly relevant to the use of the Application", and its scope may not be broadened without prior consent. Guideline 5.1.2(i): data "may only be shared with third parties to improve the app or serve advertising". Guideline 5.1.2(iii) treats data described as aggregated or anonymised as protected against re-identification. Apple's own model is the DPLA HealthKit research clause: third parties receiving de-identified data must be prohibited "from re-identifying (or attempting to re-identify)".

Announcing the sale from launch day helps with the "no broadened scope without consent" rule, but does not settle 5.1.2(i).

findings.title: UG12 needs a de-identification standard, thresholds, a no-re-identification commitment and an opt-out to be defensible
findings.where: app/legal/privacy_policy.md:15 (s2), :59 (s3.6), :116 (s9); app/legal/terms_of_service.md:48 (s8, "de-identified search queries")
findings.evidence: The documents say "aggregated or anonymised ... cannot identify you" but never define those words, set a threshold, restrict buyers or offer an objection route. ToS s8 claims ownership of row-level "de-identified search queries". Free text can contain names, phone numbers or health conditions, so removing the user id does not anonymise it. Privacy s9 keeps "de-identified comparison data" after deletion. The repo's own cohort_priors.json has cells of n=5 (e.g. 18-24|Female|Muharraq|English). OpenAI's policy promises it will "not attempt to reidentify the information, unless required by law". Google says it provides "aggregated reports to advertisers that don't reveal information about individual people".
findings.why_it_matters: Without a standard, "anonymised" is only a claim. In a small market like Bahrain, cells cut by governorate, age and gender identify people, which turns the data back into personal data, then into selling personal data, then into a data-broker or tracking problem.
findings.fix: Add the definitions and limits below (EN and AR) to s2 and s3.6. In ToS s8, replace "de-identified search queries" with "the products identified from searches". Internally: export only through a query layer that enforces k >= 50 distinct accounts per cell with complementary suppression and rounding; country-level geography (governorate only at k >= 100); at most two quasi-identifiers per table; a time window of at least a week; health, supplement and pharmacy categories never cut by demographics; an export log. Buyer contract: no re-identification, no linking with other data, no onward sale to brokers, no individual targeting or eligibility use, audit and deletion rights, the same terms passed down to anyone they share with.
findings.proposed_wording_en: s2/s3.6: "'Aggregated' means statistics combined from at least 50 different accounts, with smaller groups left out. 'Anonymised' means data that neither we nor anyone who receives it can link back to you with means reasonably likely to be used. We never sell or license individual records, the text of your searches, your photos, your profile answers or any identifier, and we never break down health-related products by age, gender or area. Anyone who receives these statistics must agree in writing not to try to identify anyone, not to combine them with other data to do so, and not to pass them to data brokers. In our legitimate interest in funding and improving MYEZ we produce these statistics and may share, license or sell them; you can object at any time by emailing privacy@getmyez.com, and we will leave your data out."

Before starting a claim, please email support@getmyez.com with "Dispute" in the subject and a description of the issue; we will reply within 30 days and try in good faith to resolve it. If we cannot, the competent courts of the Kingdom of Bahrain will decide the dispute. If you live in another country, this does not take away any right you have under the mandatory laws of that country, including the right to rely on its consumer-protection rules or to bring a claim in its courts where those laws allow.

verdicts.reason: The gap is real. AHMED_TASKS_TO_SUBMIT.md:81 still asks for the licence, the fill-in has IP_OWNER='the publisher' with the '(or are licensed to us)' fallback (legal_fill_in_u8.json:41, UL15), and nothing at 10135306 records a signed licence. The finding is overstated in three ways. (1) kind=false_statement is wrong: UL15 chose the '(or are licensed to us)' wording on purpose, and while Ahmed knowingly builds and submits the app through Hussain's account, an implied (non-written) licence by conduct is the likely reading. The sentence is undocumented, not shown false (for counsel; whether Bahraini copyright law requires writing for an exclusive licence or assignment is UNVERIFIED). (2) App Review does not ask for or check an IP licence. Apple 5.2.1 says 'owns or has licensed' and does not require a written licence, so this is not a submission gate. (3) The risk is a dispute between Ahmed and Hussain, not a user lawsuit, so medium rather than high. Recommend signing it soon (cheap, and needed before the SYNACKSOFTWARE transfer and before any data sale), but before_submission=false. The note that the ASC Developer role is access only and not a substitute is correct; role permissions remain UNVERIFIED (Apple's roles page does not clearly map 'Submit apps' to roles).

Carve-out advice stands: Civil Code art 219 (fraud/gross negligence), art 181 (prior tort exemption void) and art 58/59 are verified verbatim in the WIPO BH083 text. Two errors. (a) 'No cap' is false for the only distribution channel. Terms s16 makes Apple's standard EULA apply, and that EULA (apple.com/legal/internet-services/itunes/dev/stdeula/, Licensor = the app provider) already caps total liability at 'fifty dollars ($50.00)' and excludes personal-injury liability. The proposed BHD 50 cap would duplicate it and could conflict with it unless a precedence rule is added (see the missed EULA-conflict item). (b) The citation is wrong: art 220 of WIPO BH083 is about formal summons ('compensation shall not be due unless the debtor has been formally summoned'). The foreseeable-damages limit is art 223. Severity is low: adding carve-outs makes s12 look fair and survive art 58, but it adds no protection.

Verified that neither the EN nor the AR terms has entire-agreement, severability, no-waiver, assignment, force-majeure or mandatory-rights clauses. Assignment matters for the planned SYNACKSOFTWARE move. Overstatements: the sanctions/export point is already covered for iOS users by Apple's standard EULA (export clause, 'except as authorized by United States law'), which s16 incorporates. Also, Civil Code art 218 shows Bahraini law already treats force majeure as a default excuse unless the debtor accepts it by agreement, so the force-majeure bullet is clarifying rather than protective. The entire-agreement bullet must name Apple's EULA, or it contradicts s16.

The gap is verified: no precedence clause, and UF15 records a model review in place of a native one. Severity is overstated. Civil Code art 59 already resolves doubt in a contract of submission in the adhering party's favour, so the proposed 'more favourable to you' clause mostly restates the default and gives no real protection. The only clause that changes outcomes is 'Arabic prevails', and that needs a native legal review first. Also, ASC_SUBMISSION_PACKET_S76.md:22 (D11=B) makes the 1.0 store listing English only, which lowers exposure at launch. Low; counsel item.

s4 already says 'Use of MYEZ is free', states the current limits (matching usage_service.py TIER_LIMITS free 3/3/10), says 'We may change these limits' and says no IAP or subscriptions are sold. That is enough for the owner's 'free with rate limits' point and for App Review. The remaining gaps are real but small: no non-entitlement statement, nothing on the hidden premium tier or hand-raised review accounts, no technical rate-limit mention, no discontinuation right. Referral bonuses are in s9, not s4. Low.

Partly refuted. The terms already ban multiple accounts and farming: s3 'One account per person. Creating accounts by automated means is not allowed.', s9 withholds rewards for 'self-referral, automated sign-ups, fake accounts or coordinated rings', and s5 bans getting around usage limits, misusing servers and automated data collection. The finding's claim that s5/s3 do not ban farming is wrong. The real gaps are prompt injection, reselling or sublicensing, competing-dataset use, and misattributed shared comparisons. Useful tightening, low severity.

Verified. Privacy s4:69 confirms that OpenAI may use inputs and outputs for training on every comparison. Neither document tells users to keep people, IDs or health details out of photos and queries. The s8 licence runs to 'us' only, for operating, improving, datasets and 'to obtain comparisons from our AI provider', so OpenAI's own training use of user photos is not covered by the licence grant (it is covered only by privacy disclosure and the AI consent). The sublicence wording is the right fix. Whether health queries count as sensitive data under the GCC PDP laws is for counsel.

Verified, and stronger than stated. Besides results.dimension.dosage (en.json:223), app/services/drug_database_service.py injects the Bahrain approved-drugs table into the GPT prompt as 'ground truth for dosage, form, and ingredient details', and extraction_service.py maps supplement dose fields to 'dosage'. s6 has a one-line disclaimer only. A brand-dispute route is good practice, but the exposure is low before launch.

Partly refuted. The 'internal contradiction' is overstated. UF14 (FABLE_RULINGS_U8_FIX4_S76.md:8-11) deliberately attaches ownership to the de-identified compilation, and 'yours to view, share and delete' is an access statement about the account's history, not an ownership claim that collides with it. Claiming the compilation, not each price as a fact, is ordinary database-right style drafting. The reword is a harmless improvement. That is a counsel item gated on the first deal, not a Terms-text defect. Low.

Verified: s13 allows suspension only for breach of the Terms. The Apple EULA's automatic termination on non-compliance adds nothing beyond breach. The proposed survival list cites sections 8, 11, 12, 15 and 17, which depend on the renumbering in T-GENERAL. Low stands.

Valid as low. The finder missed that s15 (Bahrain law and courts) directly conflicts with Apple's standard EULA (California law, Santa Clara County courts, home-forum exception for EU citizens only), which s16 says 'also applies', with no precedence rule. That conflict is the bigger dispute-clause defect (listed under missed).

Art 74 is verified verbatim (WIPO BH083: void when wholly to the minor's disadvantage, annullable when mixed). Note that it governs 'contracts and other dispositions of property' by a minor with discretion. The age of majority (21) is UNVERIFIED: the WIPO text says only 'legal age'. Overstated part: demographics are optional (privacy s3.3), so 13-17 users can skip the age question; they are not forced to answer untruthfully. The missing under-18 band is a data-quality point. Privacy s12 repeats the same parent clause with no mechanism, so both documents need the same fix. Medium, counsel.
Verified that OpenAI's indemnity applies only to a 'business or organization'. Omitting a consumer indemnity follows best practice. The optional narrow clause is an owner choice. Low is correct.

Verified: en.json:286 and :750 say 'We work for you — never paid by sellers.', and s8 permits selling aggregated statistics. The claim is true today, and the risk arises only when a sale to a seller happens, so it is conditional and gated on that event. Low, not medium. The fix belongs in the pre-deal checklist.

Verified: en.json:279, 285, 544 and 749 make the '25+ retailers' claim. RETAILER_TIERS is a scoring table, and canary 7a recorded 0/2 prices, so a per-comparison count of 25 or more is UNVERIFIED and doubtful. App Review does not test this claim. Low, owner measurement.

Partly false. The live-equals-repo claim, the clickwrap text (en.json:999), TERMS_VERSION 2026-10-11 (consent_service.py:31, consent.ts:12) and the usage limits are all verified. But 's16 is adequate because ASC uses Apple's standard EULA' is wrong. That EULA (Licensor = the app provider) brings California law, Santa Clara County courts, a $50 cap, a personal-injury exclusion and a US export clause, and s15 conflicts with it on governing law and forum, with no precedence rule. Adequacy needs a precedence sentence, or a custom EULA that meets Apple's minimum terms (counsel). Also, 'every fix can land after submission without a new build' needs a qualifier: consent.ts TERMS_VERSION ships in the JS bundle, so a text change needs an OTA, and until then consent records carry the stale version (consent_service.py records the version as sent). missed: MEDIUM, counsel: Terms s16 incorporates Apple's standard EULA (ASC_SUBMISSION_PACKET_S76.md:114; apple.com/legal/internet-services/itunes/dev/stdeula/, where the Licensor is the app provider). Anything marked UNVERIFIED was not confirmed against a primary source. ## 0. Corrections to the orchestrator's facts (re-checked today) - **The getmyez.com apex is NOT behind the Cloudflare proxy any more.** It answers `Server: railway-hikari` with no cf-ray. The wildcard `*.getmyez.com` record is still proxied, and a random subdomain returns HTTP 525. - **The Ahmed Jameel invite is already done.** S77 ledger 23:10: the owner invited ahmedjameel0703@gmail.com as **Admin**, not Developer. Ahmed accepted and was added to the TestFlight group "MYEZ Internal" with build 1.0.0 (2). - The invite is **not** a submission prerequisite. The owner's question: what data can MYEZ store and sell? **What it may store today.** Everything on the published App Privacy label: 13 data types, linked to the user, no tracking. Each is defensible as long as four things hold: - it is disclosed (it is); - it is used only for the stated purposes; - it is kept for a stated period (two "no fixed period" items still need one); - it is protected (backups, rotated keys, private repo). MYEZ already collects **less** than the big companies: no ad ID, no location, no contacts, no tracking SDK. **What it may sell or license today.** Only **aggregated or anonymised statistics**, never personal data (privacy s2, ToS s8, ruling UG12). That is the same line OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Amazon publicly draw: - OpenAI says it does not sell personal data, shares de-identified data, and promises not to try to re-identify it. - Google gives advertisers aggregated reports that do not reveal individuals. - Amazon says it is "not in the business of selling" customers' personal information. Even aggregated sales sit in a grey zone under Apple's literal text: 5.1.2(i) (share only to improve the app or serve ads), 5.1.2(ii) (no repurposing without consent) and DPLA 3.3.3(B). Get counsel before the first deal. **What it may NOT do:** - sell or share row-level, event-level or pseudonymous records, including "de-identified" free-text queries, photos, profile answers or any identifier; - sell small demographic cells, for example governorate × age × gender in Bahrain (the repo's own survey has n=5 cells); - break health or supplement searches down by demographics; - sell to buyers who link the data to other data or use it for ad targeting; - send anything per user. That counts as **tracking**: it needs the ATT prompt and "Tracking = Yes" on the label, and separate explicit consent under the GCC laws. **How MYEZ compares with the big companies.** They store far more, and lawfully, because they carry the full apparatus: legal entities, data protection officers, signed DPAs, transfer mechanisms, fixed retention, per-purpose consent and opt-outs, and published no-re-identification promises. "Storing as much as big companies do" is not a legal test. The tests are purpose, legal basis, retention and security. **To go further, with counsel:** 1. Add definitions and thresholds to the documents (section 6 block S6). 2. Export only through a query layer that enforces at least 50 accounts per cell, with suppression and an export log. 3. Sign a buyer contract that bans re-identification, linking with other data and onward sale. 4. Offer users an opt-out of statistics. 5. Write a legitimate-interest assessment and a DPIA. 6.
